records.source: Ἐὰν ταῖς γλώσσαις τῶν ἀνθρώπων λαλῶ καὶ τῶν ἀγγέλων, ἀγάπην δὲ μὴ ἔχω, γέγονα χαλκὸς ἠχῶν ἢ κύμβαλον ἀλαλάζον.
records.gloss: If in the tongues of the men I speak and of the angels, love but not I have, I have become bronze echoing or cymbal clanging.
pieces: Suppose I speak in the tongues of {{gender:human beings|men}}, and of angels too. If I do not have love, I am no more than booming bronze or a clashing cymbal.

L.1: If I speak in the tongues of {{gender:human beings|men}} and of angels, but do not have love, I have become echoing bronze or a clanging cymbal.

R.1: I might be able to speak in tongues, in the languages of people and even of angels. But if I do not have love, I am only empty noise, like banging metal or a crashing cymbal.

decisions.choice: tongues of human beings and of angels: the gift of tongues of 12:10, pictured at its very highest, speech in any human language and even in the language of angels
alternatives: eloquence in many human languages, with no reference to the gift
decisions.reason: Chapter 13 continues from 12:31 and takes up the gifts just listed, starting with the one the Corinthians prized most (14:1-25). γλώσσαις means both the tongue and a language. Some Jewish writings of the time speak of angels having their own language (the Testament of Job describes Job's daughters speaking in it), and some in Corinth may have thought their tongues were the speech of angels. Paul names the highest gift he can imagine in order to say that even this is nothing without love.

decisions.choice: if I speak: a supposed case, with Paul using himself as the example
decisions.reason: Ἐὰν with the subjunctive sets up a supposition, not a claim. In verses 1-3 Paul puts himself in the place of the most gifted person imaginable, so that no reader can think the rule applies only to others. He does speak in tongues (14:18), but the point is the supposition, not his experience.

decisions.choice: love: the self-giving care for others that God shows, which seeks their good rather than one's own
decisions.reason: ἀγάπην is the word Paul uses for God's love in Christ (Romans 5:8; 2 Corinthians 5:14) and for the love believers owe one another (8:1). Verses 4-7 describe it by what it does and does not do. It is not a feeling or a gift alongside the others but the way every gift is to be used (12:31; 14:1).

decisions.choice: echoing bronze and a clanging cymbal: loud metal instruments or objects that make noise without meaning
alternatives: a sounding jar in a theater
decisions.reason: χαλκὸς is bronze, and ἠχῶν means sounding or echoing; the phrase may describe a bronze gong, bronze instruments in general, or the bronze vessels said to have been set in theaters to carry the sound. Corinth was famous in the ancient world for its bronze. κύμβαλον is a cymbal, and ἀλαλάζον is used of loud wailing or crying out. Cymbals and gongs were played in the worship of pagan gods such as Cybele and Dionysus, which the Corinthians knew. The point is that speech without love is noise, however impressive.

decisions.choice: I have become: the perfect tense describes the state that results; I am now nothing but noise
decisions.reason: γέγονα is a perfect. It does not describe a change at some past moment but what the speaker is: if the condition is met, that is what he has turned into.

decisions.choice: love (L, B, R), here and throughout the chapter
decisions.reason: The King James Version says "charity" in this chapter, following the Latin word caritas. In modern English "charity" means giving to the poor or an organization that does so, which verse 3 shows is not what Paul means. "Love" is used at every level.

decisions.choice: {{gender:human beings|men}}
decisions.reason: ἀνθρώπων here means people in general, set against angels, so the inclusive form is the default and "men" the alternative.

decisions.choice: speak in tongues, in the languages of people (R); I am only empty noise, like banging metal or a crashing cymbal (R)
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the name of the gift, "tongues", and adds "languages" to explain it (m1). It says what the picture means, empty noise (m4), and uses "banging metal" because a bronze object would be unfamiliar.

records.heading: Without love, nothing

records.source: καὶ ἐὰν ἔχω προφητείαν καὶ εἰδῶ τὰ μυστήρια πάντα καὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γνῶσιν, καὶ ἐὰν ἔχω πᾶσαν τὴν πίστιν ὥστε ὄρη μεθιστάναι, ἀγάπην δὲ μὴ ἔχω, οὐθέν εἰμι.
records.gloss: And if I have prophecy and know the mysteries all and all the knowledge, and if I have all the faith so as mountains to move, love but not I have, nothing I am.
pieces: I may be able to prophesy, and know every mystery and everything there is to know; I may have all the faith there is, enough to move mountains; but if I do not have love, I am nothing.

L.2: And if I have prophecy and know all the mysteries and all the knowledge, and if I have all the faith, so as to move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing.

R.2: I might be able to prophesy. I might understand every mystery of God and know everything there is to know. I might have so much faith that I could tell mountains to move, and they would move. But if I do not have love, I am nothing.

decisions.choice: have prophecy: have the gift of prophecy, speaking a message from God for the church
decisions.reason: προφητείαν is the gift of 12:10 and 12:28, the one Paul ranks highest in chapter 14 because it builds up the church (14:1-5). To "have" it is to have been given the gift.

decisions.choice: know all the mysteries and all knowledge: understand every part of God's hidden purposes and all that can be known of them
decisions.reason: μυστήρια are God's purposes once hidden and now revealed (2:1, 7; 4:1; 15:51). γνῶσιν is the gift of 12:8, prized in Corinth (8:1). "All" is said twice: Paul imagines the gift with no limit at all.

decisions.choice: all faith: the special gift of faith of 12:9, confidence that God will act, at its fullest
decisions.reason: Every believer has faith in Christ, but here πίστιν is the gift given only to some (12:9), and πᾶσαν pictures it with nothing lacking. The key term "faith" is kept.

decisions.choice: so as to move mountains: an echo of Jesus' saying about faith that can move a mountain
decisions.reason: Jesus said that faith could tell a mountain to be lifted up and thrown into the sea (Mark 11:23; Matthew 17:20; 21:21). Paul uses the saying to describe faith that can do what seems impossible.

decisions.choice: I am nothing: worth nothing in God's sight, not merely without benefit
decisions.reason: οὐθέν εἰμι is stronger than verse 3, "I gain nothing". The person with the greatest gifts but no love does not just lose something; in what counts before God, he is nothing (compare 3:7, where Paul says that the planter and waterer are nothing).

decisions.choice: I may be able to prophesy (B); I might be able to prophesy (R)
alternatives: I may have the gift of prophecy
decisions.reason: "Have prophecy" is not natural English. Balanced and Readable say it with the verb; the gift is the same (m1).

decisions.choice: every mystery of God; I could tell mountains to move, and they would move
decisions.reason: Readable says whose mysteries they are (m2) and spells out the saying of Jesus behind the picture (m4). "Mystery" is the settled key term and is kept.

records.source: καὶ ἐὰν ψωμίσω πάντα τὰ ὑπάρχοντά μου, καὶ ἐὰν παραδῶ τὸ σῶμά μου, ἵνα καυθήσομαι, ἀγάπην δὲ μὴ ἔχω, οὐδὲν ὠφελοῦμαι.
records.gloss: And if I give away in food all the possessions of me, and if I hand over the body of me so that I will be burned, love but not I have, nothing I am benefited.
pieces: I may hand out everything I own as food for others; I may hand over my body to the flames; but if I do not have love, it does me no good at all.

L.3: And if I give away all my possessions as food, and if I hand over my body so that I will be burned, but do not have love, I am benefited nothing.

R.3: I might give away everything I own to feed hungry people. I might even give up my life and let them burn my body. But if I do not have love, it does me no good.

decisions.choice: so that I will be burned, as the SBLGNT reads; manuscripts are divided between this and "so that I may boast"
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT reads καυθήσομαι, "I will be burned". From general knowledge: several of the oldest manuscripts, including the early papyrus P46 and the codices Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Vaticanus, read a word that differs by one letter, "so that I may boast"; many later manuscripts and early translations read forms of "be burned". "Boast" is the harder reading and would mean giving up one's body to win a reason for pride; Paul elsewhere speaks of boasting in a good sense (9:15-16). "Be burned" fits the climax of the list and was understood this way by many early writers, but its odd grammar may show it is a correction. Reviewers must check the SBLGNT apparatus before this sentence is marked meaning reviewed.

decisions.choice: give away all my possessions as food: hand out everything one owns, bit by bit, to feed others
decisions.reason: ψωμίσω means to feed, especially by giving out food in small portions. Paul pictures someone who gives away every last thing to feed the poor, the greatest act of generosity he can name.

decisions.choice: hand over my body to be burned: give up one's life by fire, as a martyr
alternatives: sell oneself into slavery to help others
decisions.reason: The phrase recalls the three young men in Daniel 3, who gave up their bodies to the fire rather than worship an idol (Daniel 3:28), a story Jews of Paul's day told of those faithful to death. Some have thought instead of selling oneself as a slave, whose body was branded; that suits the reading "so that I may boast" better (m1).

decisions.choice: I gain nothing: it brings me no benefit before God
decisions.reason: ὠφελοῦμαι is passive, "I am benefited". The others may be helped by the gifts and the sacrifice, but the giver without love gains nothing from them on the day God judges (3:13-15; 4:5).

decisions.choice: hand over my body to the flames (B); give up my life and let them burn my body (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable follow the SBLGNT reading (m1) and say plainly that the person dies by fire (m3); the footnote gives "so that I may boast".

decisions.choice: to feed hungry people
decisions.reason: Readable says who is fed (m2).

records.source: Ἡ ἀγάπη μακροθυμεῖ, χρηστεύεται ἡ ἀγάπη, οὐ ζηλοῖ ἡ ἀγάπη, οὐ περπερεύεται, οὐ φυσιοῦται, οὐκ ἀσχημονεῖ, οὐ ζητεῖ τὰ ἑαυτῆς, οὐ παροξύνεται, οὐ λογίζεται τὸ κακόν, οὐ χαίρει ἐπὶ τῇ ἀδικίᾳ, συγχαίρει δὲ τῇ ἀληθείᾳ·
records.gloss: The love is patient, is kind the love, not envies the love, not brags, not is puffed up, \v 5 not behaves improperly, not seeks the [things] of itself, not is provoked, not reckons the evil, \v 6 not rejoices over the unrighteousness, rejoices with but the truth;
pieces: Love is patient; love is kind. Love does not envy, does not show off, is not puffed up.
It does not behave shamefully, it does not look for its own advantage, it does not lose its temper, and it does not keep a tally of wrongs.
It takes no pleasure in wrongdoing, but shares the joy of the truth.

L.4: Love is patient, love is kind, love does not envy, does not brag, is not puffed up,
L.5: does not behave improperly, does not seek its own [things], is not provoked, does not reckon the wrong,
L.6: does not rejoice over unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth.

R.4: Love is patient with others and kind to them. Love does not envy others. It does not brag, and it does not act proud.
R.5: It does not treat people rudely. It does not put itself first. It does not lose its temper. It does not keep thinking about the wrongs others have done to it.
R.6: It is not happy about wrongdoing, but it is glad about what is true.

decisions.choice: love is described by verbs: what it does and what it does not do
decisions.reason: Paul does not define love; in verses 4-7 he describes it with fifteen verbs, as if it were a person. Most of the verbs are negative, and several name faults Paul has already rebuked in Corinth: jealousy (3:3), being puffed up (4:6, 18-19; 5:2; 8:1), seeking one's own advantage (10:24, 33) and behaving shamefully at the Lord's Supper (11:20-22). The portrait is also a portrait of Christ, who did all these things for others.

decisions.choice: patient, kind: slow to anger with others, and active in doing them good
decisions.reason: μακροθυμεῖ means to bear long with others and not strike back; χρηστεύεται is to show kindness, to be generous and useful to others. Paul joins God's patience and kindness in Romans 2:4, and lists the two side by side as fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22).

decisions.choice: does not envy, does not brag, is not puffed up: free of rivalry and self-display
decisions.reason: ζηλοῖ is the verb of 12:31 and 14:1, used here in its bad sense, to envy, as its noun is in 3:3. περπερεύεται occurs only here in the New Testament and means to talk oneself up, to show off. φυσιοῦται is the verb for being puffed up that Paul uses through the letter (4:6; 8:1).

decisions.choice: does not behave shamefully, does not seek its own: does not act in ways that disgrace itself or others, and does not pursue its own advantage
decisions.reason: ἀσχημονεῖ is to behave improperly or disgracefully (7:36; compare 12:23). ζητεῖ τὰ ἑαυτῆς repeats Paul's rule in 10:24 and 10:33: seek the good of others, not your own.

decisions.choice: is not provoked: does not become angry or irritated
decisions.reason: παροξύνεται is to be stirred to anger (Acts 17:16). Love does not let other people's faults make it bitter.

decisions.choice: does not keep account of wrongs: does not count up the wrong done to it or hold it against the one who did it
alternatives: does not plot evil, does not plan harm to others
decisions.reason: λογίζεται is a word for reckoning and keeping accounts; Paul uses it in 2 Corinthians 5:19 for God "not counting their trespasses against them". On this reading love keeps no record of wrongs suffered. The same words can also mean to plan harm: Zechariah 8:17 in the Greek Old Testament tells Israel not to devise evil against a neighbor in their hearts. Both readings fit; the accounting sense matches the verbs of patience around it.

decisions.choice: rejoices with the truth: shares in the joy when the truth prevails, as if truth were a person
decisions.reason: ἀδικίᾳ (wrongdoing, injustice) and ἀληθείᾳ are set against each other, as in Romans 2:8. Truth here is not only accurate statements but what is right and true, including the truth of the gospel. συγχαίρει means to rejoice together with someone; love and truth are glad together.

decisions.choice: the list is kept as verbs: love is patient, love is kind, does not envy, does not brag
decisions.reason: The Greek uses verbs, not adjectives, so each level says what love does. The opening words, "love is patient, love is kind", are what the Greek says and cannot be put more simply; they are kept although they are familiar. Readable spells out the objects ("with others", "to them").

decisions.choice: does not brag (L, R), does not show off (B); puffed up (L, B), proud (R)
decisions.reason: "Boast" is kept for a different word family in this letter (1:29-31; 13:3 footnote), so this rare verb is "brag" or "show off". The verb for being puffed up has the settled wording for 1 Corinthians.

decisions.choice: does not behave shamefully (B), does not treat people rudely (R); does not lose its temper (B, R)
decisions.reason: Plain words for improper behavior (m4) and for being provoked to anger (m5). "Easily" is not added; the Greek says love is not provoked at all.

decisions.choice: does not reckon the wrong (L); does not keep a tally of wrongs (B); does not keep thinking about the wrongs others have done to it (R)
decisions.reason: Each level gives the accounting sense chosen in m6; the footnote gives "does not plot evil".

decisions.choice: shares the joy of the truth (B); is glad about what is true (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the picture of rejoicing together (m7); Readable says it simply.

records.source: πάντα στέγει, πάντα πιστεύει, πάντα ἐλπίζει, πάντα ὑπομένει.
records.gloss: All things it bears, all things it believes, all things it hopes, all things it endures.
pieces: There is nothing love cannot bear, no time when it stops believing or hoping, nothing it cannot endure.

L.7: All things it bears, all things it believes, all things it hopes, all things it endures.

R.7: Love puts up with anything. It keeps believing and keeps hoping, whatever happens. It keeps going through every trouble.

decisions.choice: bears: puts up with whatever comes, as Paul says of himself in 9:12
alternatives: covers, does not expose the faults of others
decisions.reason: στέγει first meant to cover, as a roof covers and keeps out the rain, and so to bear up or to put up with something. In 9:12 Paul uses it for putting up with every hardship for the gospel's sake. Some read it here as "covers", keeping quiet about others' faults (compare 1 Peter 4:8), or as "protects"; but the last verb of the verse would then not be the only one about bearing hardship.

decisions.choice: believes, hopes: love does not give up trust and hope, in God and for others
alternatives: love always believes the best about people
decisions.reason: πιστεύει does not mean that love believes anything it is told; Paul calls for testing what is said (12:10; 14:29). Love keeps trusting God and is ready to think the best of others, and it keeps hoping for what God will do. The verbs prepare for verse 13, where faith and hope stand with love.

decisions.choice: all things: in every situation, with no limit
decisions.reason: πάντα stands first four times for emphasis. It describes how far love goes, not a rule that love accepts every claim or every wrong (verse 6 says it takes no pleasure in wrongdoing).

decisions.choice: endures: holds out under hardship without giving way
decisions.reason: ὑπομένει is the verb of the noun for endurance (2 Corinthians 1:6; 6:4). Love does not give up when things go hard.

decisions.choice: All things it bears, all things it believes ... (L)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Greek order, which puts "all things" first each time for emphasis (m3).

decisions.choice: There is nothing love cannot bear ... (B); puts up with anything ... keeps going through every trouble (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "all things" as English says it, and turn the verbs into plain words for bearing, trusting, hoping and holding out (m1-m4). "Believing" keeps the key term.

pieces: Love never comes to an end.

decisions.choice: never falls: never collapses or comes to an end
decisions.reason: πίπτει means to fall. Set against the gifts that will be set aside (verses 8-10), it means that love never falls away or passes out of use. It could also mean that love never fails in what it does, but the contrast with what ends points to lasting.

decisions.choice: falls, as the SBLGNT reads
decisions.reason: From general knowledge: many later manuscripts read a compound form of the same verb, "falls away", with the same meaning. Reviewers must check the SBLGNT apparatus before this sentence is marked meaning reviewed.

decisions.choice: comes to an end (B); will never stop (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "never falls" means here (m1). Literal keeps "falls".

records.heading: Love never comes to an end

records.source: εἴτε δὲ προφητεῖαι, καταργηθήσονται· εἴτε γλῶσσαι, παύσονται· εἴτε γνῶσις, καταργηθήσεται.
records.gloss: Whether but prophecies, they will be set aside; whether tongues, they will cease; whether knowledge, it will be set aside.
pieces: But prophecies will be done away with; tongues will fall silent; knowledge will be done away with.

L.8: But if [there are] prophecies, they will be set aside; if tongues, they will cease; if knowledge, it will be set aside.

R.8: But prophecy is not going to last. Speaking in tongues will stop. The gift of knowledge is not going to last.

decisions.choice: whether there are prophecies, tongues or knowledge: whatever gifts there may be, all of them are temporary
decisions.reason: εἴτε repeated three times sets the gifts side by side: however much of them there is, each will end. They are three of the gifts named in 12:8-10 and in verses 1-2.

decisions.choice: will be set aside: will be brought to an end, no longer in use, with God as the one who ends them
decisions.reason: καταργηθήσονται is passive and is the verb Paul uses for what God brings to an end (1:28; 2:6; 15:24, 26). It returns in verse 10 for the partial and in verse 11 for childhood. The gifts are not bad; they belong to the present time.

decisions.choice: will cease: will stop
alternatives: tongues will stop of their own accord, earlier than the other gifts
decisions.reason: Paul uses a different verb for tongues, παύσονται. Some read the middle voice as meaning that tongues will die out of themselves, before the others; but Paul probably varies the verb for style, and verse 10 gives one time for all the partial gifts to end.

decisions.choice: knowledge: the gift of 12:8, knowledge of God's ways given by the Spirit
decisions.reason: Not all knowing ends (verse 12 promises full knowledge); what ends is the partial knowledge given now (verse 9).

decisions.choice: set aside (L); done away with (B); not going to last (R)
decisions.reason: The same wording as for this verb in 2 Corinthians 3, so that readers can follow it; it returns in verses 10 and 11.

decisions.choice: speaking in tongues; the gift of knowledge
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that the gifts are meant (m4).

records.source: ἐκ μέρους γὰρ γινώσκομεν καὶ ἐκ μέρους προφητεύομεν·
records.gloss: In part for we know and in part we prophesy;
pieces: For what we know is only partial, and our prophesying is partial too.

L.9: For in part we know, and in part we prophesy.

R.9: What we know now is not complete. What we say when we prophesy is not complete either.

decisions.choice: in part: partially, incompletely
decisions.reason: ἐκ μέρους means "in part". In 12:27 the same phrase meant "individually"; here it is set against the complete of verse 10, so it means that what we know and prophesy is not the whole.

decisions.choice: we know, we prophesy: all believers, Paul included
decisions.reason: Paul includes himself, an apostle with many gifts (14:18). Even the best knowledge and prophecy now given is partial.

decisions.choice: in part we know, and in part we prophesy (L)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Greek order, which puts "in part" first for emphasis.

records.source: ὅταν δὲ ἔλθῃ τὸ τέλειον, τὸ ἐκ μέρους καταργηθήσεται.
records.gloss: When but comes the complete, the in part will be set aside.
pieces: But when what is complete arrives, what is partial will be done away with.

L.10: But when the complete comes, what is in part will be set aside.

R.10: But when what is complete comes, the things that are only partial are not going to last.

decisions.choice: the complete: what is whole and finished, as opposed to what is in part
decisions.reason: τέλειον means complete, whole, or full-grown (2:6; 14:20). Here it is the opposite of ἐκ μέρους "in part" (verse 9), so "complete" is its sense; verse 11 adds the picture of growing up.

decisions.choice: the complete comes when Christ returns and believers see God face to face
decisions.reason: Verse 12 says when the partial ends: "then", when we see "face to face" and know as we are known. That points to the end of this age, when Christ comes (1:7-8; 15:23-28). Others have taken the complete to be the finished New Testament, or the church grown mature, or love itself; but the face to face sight of verse 12 is not yet given in this life.

decisions.choice: will be set aside: will come to an end, no longer needed
decisions.reason: καταργηθήσεται is the verb of verse 8. The partial gifts end not because they fail but because what they pointed to has come.

decisions.choice: the complete (L); what is complete (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Perfect" now suggests without fault; the Greek word here means whole, set against "in part" (m1). The footnote gives "the perfect".

records.source: ὅτε ἤμην νήπιος, ἐλάλουν ὡς νήπιος, ἐφρόνουν ὡς νήπιος, ἐλογιζόμην ὡς νήπιος· ὅτε γέγονα ἀνήρ, κατήργηκα τὰ τοῦ νηπίου.
records.gloss: When I was a child, I used to speak as a child, I used to think as a child, I used to reason as a child; when I have become a man, I have set aside the [things] of the child.
pieces: When I was a child, I talked as a child talks, thought as a child thinks, and reasoned as a child reasons. But I am a man now, and I have done away with childish ways.

L.11: When I was a child, I used to speak like a child, I used to think like a child, I used to reason like a child; now that I have become a man, I have set aside the [things] of the child.

R.11: When I was a little child, I spoke, thought and reasoned the way little children do. But now I am grown up, and I have stopped acting like a child.

decisions.choice: child: a young child, not yet grown
decisions.reason: νήπιος is a small child or infant, the word Paul used in 3:1 for the Corinthians as "infants in Christ". Here it is used without blame: every adult was once a child.

decisions.choice: I used to speak, think and reason; I have become, I have set aside: the past habits of childhood against a lasting change
decisions.reason: The first three verbs are imperfects, describing what a child does again and again. γέγονα and κατήργηκα are perfects: the change is complete and its result remains.

decisions.choice: think, reason: a child's outlook and the way it weighs things
alternatives: speak, think and reason correspond to tongues, prophecy and knowledge
decisions.reason: ἐφρόνουν is to think, to have a mind set on something; ἐλογιζόμην is to reason or count things up. Some see the three verbs as matching tongues, prophecy and knowledge in verse 8, but Paul does not say so.

decisions.choice: the picture explains verse 10: the present gifts belong to a time of growing up, and the end will be like becoming an adult
decisions.reason: κατήργηκα is the verb of verses 8 and 10. Paul is not telling the Corinthians to put away the gifts now; in chapter 14 he tells them to seek them (14:1, 39). The present age compared with the age to come is like childhood compared with adulthood.

decisions.choice: a man (L, B), grown up (R); set aside (L), done away with (B), stopped (R)
decisions.reason: Paul speaks of himself, so "man" takes no gender setting; Readable says "grown up", the point of the picture. The verb has the wording used in verses 8 and 10; Readable says simply that he stopped acting like a child. Literal says "now that I have become" to show that both verbs of the second half are perfects (m2).

records.source: βλέπομεν γὰρ ἄρτι δι’ ἐσόπτρου ἐν αἰνίγματι, τότε δὲ πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον· ἄρτι γινώσκω ἐκ μέρους, τότε δὲ ἐπιγνώσομαι καθὼς καὶ ἐπεγνώσθην.
records.gloss: We see for now through a mirror in a riddle, then but face to face; now I know in part, then but I will know fully just as also I was fully known.
pieces: For now we see by means of a mirror, as if in a riddle, but then we will see face to face. Now my knowledge is partial, but then I will know fully, as God has fully known me.

L.12: For now we see through a mirror, in a riddle, but then face to face; now I know in part, but then I will know fully, just as I also was fully known.

R.12: Right now it is as if we are looking into a mirror that does not show things clearly. But one day we will see face to face. Right now I know only part of what there is to know. But then I will know fully, in the same way that God already knows me fully.

decisions.choice: a mirror: a polished metal mirror, which showed a real but indirect image
alternatives: a window of thin stone or glass
decisions.reason: Ancient mirrors were made of polished metal, often bronze, for which Corinth was well known. They showed a true image, but only a reflection, never the thing itself. The contrast is between seeing indirectly and seeing directly, not between a true and a false image.

decisions.choice: in a riddle ... face to face: an echo of God's words about Moses in Numbers 12:8
decisions.reason: In Numbers 12:8 God says that with Moses he speaks mouth to mouth, plainly and not in riddles; the Greek Old Testament uses the same noun as αἰνίγματι. Moses spoke with God "face to face" (Exodus 33:11). Now, Paul says, all believers see God only indirectly, as in a riddle; then they will see as Moses was given to see, and more.

decisions.choice: then: at the end, when Christ comes, believers will see God directly
decisions.reason: ἄρτι and τότε set the present age against the age to come (verse 10). Seeing "face to face" is the hope of seeing God himself (Matthew 5:8; 1 John 3:2; Revelation 22:4).

decisions.choice: I will know fully just as I was fully known: I will know God as fully as God has known me
decisions.reason: ἐπιγνώσομαι and ἐπεγνώσθην are formed from the verb for "know" in this verse with a prefix that strengthens it, set against "in part". The passive ἐπεγνώσθην has God as the one who knows, as in 8:3 and Galatians 4:9. God's knowledge of his people, which is also his choosing and love, comes first; their full knowledge of him is the goal.

decisions.choice: we will see (B, R); God has fully known me (B); God already knows me fully (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek leaves out the verb in "then face to face" and the one who knows in "I was fully known"; Balanced and Readable supply them (m3, m4).

decisions.choice: through a mirror, in a riddle (L); by means of a mirror, as if in a riddle (B); a mirror that does not show things clearly (R)
decisions.reason: "Riddle" keeps the link with Numbers 12:8 (m2). The familiar "through a glass, darkly" of the King James Version used "glass" for a mirror; "darkly" is footnoted as the alternative.

records.source: νυνὶ δὲ μένει πίστις, ἐλπίς, ἀγάπη· τὰ τρία ταῦτα, μείζων δὲ τούτων ἡ ἀγάπη.
records.gloss: Now but remains faith, hope, love, the three these; greater but of these the love.
pieces: As things are, then, three things last: faith, hope and love. And of these three, the greatest is love.

L.13: But now faith, hope, love remain, these three; but the greatest of these [is] love.

R.13: So three things last: faith, hope and love. And the greatest of the three is love.

decisions.choice: but now: as things are, in contrast with the gifts that end
decisions.reason: νυνὶ can mark time ("now, in this present life") or logic ("but as it is"), as in 12:18. Read as logic, faith, hope and love last beyond the end of the gifts, into the age to come. Read as time, they are what lasts now, before the end, and only love goes on forever, since faith will become sight and hope will be fulfilled (2 Corinthians 5:7; Romans 8:24). The contrast with the passing gifts of verse 8 favors the logical sense, but the other is possible.

decisions.choice: remain: last, continue, in contrast with the gifts that are set aside
decisions.reason: μένει means to stay or last (3:14; 2 Corinthians 3:11). It is singular, though it has three subjects: the three stand together as one whole.

decisions.choice: faith, hope and love: three marks of the Christian life that Paul often names together
decisions.reason: The same three appear in 1 Thessalonians 1:3 and 5:8, Galatians 5:5-6 and Colossians 1:4-5. Here πίστις is the faith of every believer, not the special gift of verse 2.

decisions.choice: the greatest: a comparative form used for the highest of three
decisions.reason: μείζων is the comparative form, "greater". In the Greek of Paul's day the comparative was often used for the highest of more than two, so with three items the sense is "the greatest".

decisions.choice: love is the greatest because it is God's own love and the goal of the others
decisions.reason: Paul does not say why. The chapter shows that love gives every gift its worth (verses 1-3) and never ends (verse 8). Faith and hope look to God; love is what God himself shows (Romans 5:5, 8), and faith itself works through love (Galatians 5:6).

decisions.choice: last (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Remain" (Literal) is kept for the form; Balanced and Readable use the plain word "last" (m2).

decisions.choice: the greatest of these [is] love (L); of these three, the greatest is love (B); the greatest of the three is love (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek says this and little else can be said; the wording is familiar because it is close to the Greek. Literal brackets the verb the Greek leaves out.
